      "verbatim": "At the whole transcriptome level, the comparison of DEGs between murine models and human data showed relatively modest alignment rates (approximately 50%) when considering only fold changes and the direction of regulation for all models."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "agreement rate",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "the proportion of differentially expressed genes and differentially regulated pathways that were statistically modulated and in the same direction, focusing on statistically significant findings in humans.",
      "compared": "murine models vs human data",
      "species": [
        "mouse",
        "human"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": "genes and pathways",
      "verbatim": "However, when focusing on statistically significant findings in humans (DEGs and DRPs) characterizing ‘early disease development’, ‘all disease stages’ and ‘disease progression’ (as detailed in the Methods ), we observed an improved and statistically significant agreement for the majority of murine models."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "agreement rate",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "the proportion of differentially regulated pathways that showed a high level of agreement with human data.",
      "compared": "murine models vs human data",
      "species": [
        "mouse",
        "human"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": "pathways",
      "verbatim": "The DRPs (shown in Fig. 3 ) demonstrated a high level of agreement with human data, with only a few exceptions, as detailed in Fig. 4 ."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "agreement rate",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "the proportion of models that closely recapitulated the burden of ‘early disease development’ (metabolic) differentially regulated pathway changes observed in human subjects.",
      "compared": "murine models vs human data",
      "species": [
        "mouse",
        "human"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": "models",
      "verbatim": "Despite these similarities, very few models (mainly HFD, WD and HFD/WD2%-AMLD and LDLR-CDHFHCD) closely recapitulated (with >90% agreement) the burden of ‘early disease development’ (metabolic) DRP changes observed in human subjects."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "congruence rate",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "the proportion of models that achieved the highest congruence with human MASLD at the transcriptomic level.",
      "compared": "murine models vs human data",
      "species": [
        "mouse",
        "human"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": "models",
      "verbatim": "This demonstrates that WD, WDAMLD and most choline-deficient dietary models achieve the highest congruence with human MASLD at the transcriptomic level."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "agreement rate",
      "value": null,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "the proportion of models that generally replicate the gene expression dysregulation observed in progressive human MASH.",
      "compared": "murine models vs human data",
      "species": [
        "mouse",
        "human"
      ],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": "models",
      "verbatim": "These transcriptomics data suggest that most models (apart from GMCHOW, HFD and HFDAMLD, and some choline-deficient models) generally replicate the gene expression dysregulation observed in progressive human MASH."
    }
  ],
  "headline_index": null,
  "what_the_study_did": "The study retrospectively analyzed and ranked common murine MASLD models based on their similarity to human MASLD, integrating metabolic phenotype, liver histology, and liver transcriptome data.",
  "what_it_found": "The study identified specific murine models, particularly those using Western diets, that closely mimic various aspects of human MASLD, while acknowledging that no single model perfectly replicates all features of the disease.",
  "key_quotes": [
    {
      "quote": "Our approach identified murine MASLD models showing (phenotypic and/or histologic and/or transcriptomic) profiles relevant to human MASH, which are suitable for most preclinical experimental applications.",
      "topic": "Model relevance"
    },
    {
      "quote": "At the whole transcriptome level, the comparison of DEGs between murine models and human data showed relatively modest alignment rates (approximately 50%) when considering only fold changes and the direction of regulation for all models.",
      "topic": "Transcriptome alignment"
    },
    {
      "quote": "The DRPs (shown in Fig. 3 ) demonstrated a high level of agreement with human data, with only a few exceptions, as detailed in Fig. 4 .",
      "topic": "Pathway agreement"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Despite these similarities, very few models (mainly HFD, WD and HFD/WD2%-AMLD and LDLR-CDHFHCD) closely recapitulated (with >90% agreement) the burden of ‘early disease development’ (metabolic) DRP changes observed in human subjects.",
      "topic": "Metabolic recapitulation"
    },
    {
      "quote": "These transcriptomics data suggest that most models (apart from GMCHOW, HFD and HFDAMLD, and some choline-deficient models) generally replicate the gene expression dysregulation observed in progressive human MASH.",
      "topic": "Gene expression"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Our study provides several important outcomes and unique insights. A key strength of our study lies in the uniformity of methodology applied across all models for staining and scoring liver histopathology.",
      "topic": "Histopathology methodology"
    }
  ]
}
